advances: The proposed uniform scalar coefficient \(1/2\) is false. The finite exact witness is \(m=6\), \(\theta=\log 2\), with \(F(6,\log 2)=423505/861273<1/2\). The reflection/Cauchy lower bound itself is valid on log-affine Cartesian interval supports and factors as \(M_1(p)\ge\frac14\prod_i F(m_i,\theta_i)\). On Cartesian powers of the witness, this particular lower-bound expression loses the factor \((847010/861273)^N\) relative to \(2^{-N}/4\), and its Jensen consequence loses the cube of that factor relative to \(8^{-N}/64\). This refutes the required scalar bridge, not either proposed moment bound for the actual depths and not the locked mixed-integer conjecture.

proof:
First, \(0\le j-r_j\le j+r_j\le m-1\), so every summand defining \(B_j\) is a valid interval site. Since the law is strictly positive, \(B_j>0\). Directly from the exponential formula, \(p_{j+u}=p_j e^{\theta u}\). Hence \(B_j=p_j\sum_{u=-r_j}^{r_j}e^{\theta u}\), proving the stated equivalence without division by \(\theta\) or by \(e^\theta-1\). It therefore includes \(\theta=0\) and every finite interval length. At either endpoint \(r_j=0\), so \(k_j=1\), \(B_j=p_j\), and its contribution to \(F\) is exactly \(p_j^2\).

Reversing the finite geometric sum gives \(Z(-\theta)=e^{-\theta(m-1)}Z(\theta)\), and thus \(p_j(-\theta)=p_{m-1-j}(\theta)\). Also \(r_j=r_{m-1-j}\), and reversing the summation interval gives \(B_j(-\theta)=B_{m-1-j}(\theta)\). Reindexing the sum for \(F\) proves evenness in \(\theta\), so no sign restriction is being imposed. When \(m=1\), the only site has \(p_0=B_0=k_0=1\), proving \(F(1,\theta)=1\).

At \(\theta=0\), \(p_j=1/m\) and \(B_j=k_j/m\), so \(F(m,0)=m^{-2}\sum_j k_j\). If \(m=2h\), the values \(1,3,\ldots,2h-1\) occur twice, giving \(\sum_j k_j=2h^2=m^2/2\). If \(m=2h+1\), those same values occur twice and the central value is \(2h+1\), giving \(\sum_j k_j=2h^2+2h+1=(m^2+1)/2\). This includes \(h=0\) in the odd case.

Now choose the exact geometric ratio \(\rho=2\), so \(\theta=\log 2\), and \(m=6\). The original normalization is \(Z=1+2+4+8+16+32=63\), so \(p_j=2^j/63\). The following table evaluates every term directly from its original centered interval; the last column is the term in \(F\) multiplied by \(3969=63^2\).

| \(j\) | \(r_j\) | \(k_j\) | \(63p_j\) | \(63B_j\) | \(3969k_j^2p_j^3/B_j\) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 3 | 2 | 7 | \(72/7\) |
| 2 | 2 | 5 | 4 | 31 | \(1600/31\) |
| 3 | 2 | 5 | 8 | 62 | \(6400/31\) |
| 4 | 1 | 3 | 16 | 56 | \(4608/7\) |
| 5 | 0 | 1 | 32 | 32 | 1024 |

Indeed, the nontrivial interval sums in \(63B_j\) are \(1+2+4=7\), \(1+2+4+8+16=31\), \(2+4+8+16+32=62\), and \(8+16+32=56\). Every last-column entry is \(k_j^2(2^j)^3/(63B_j)\). Summing gives the exact computation

\[
\begin{aligned}
F(6,\log 2)
&=\frac1{3969}\left(1025+\frac{4680}{7}+\frac{8000}{31}\right)\\
&=\frac{1025\cdot217+4680\cdot31+8000\cdot7}{3969\cdot217}
=\frac{423505}{861273},\\
\frac12-F(6,\log 2)
&=\frac{861273-2\cdot423505}{2\cdot861273}
=\frac{14263}{1722546}>0.
\end{aligned}
\]

An independent check uses the second definition of \(F\): its shifted exponential denominators for radii \(0,1,2\) are respectively \(1\), \(1/2+1+2=7/2\), and \(1/4+1/2+1+2+4=31/4\). Pairing roots with equal radii therefore gives

\[
F(6,\log 2)
=\frac1{3969}\left[
(1+1024)+\frac{9(4+256)}{7/2}+\frac{25(16+64)}{31/4}
\right],
\]

which is exactly the same rational value. Thus the witness satisfies both original formulations and all boundary constraints. Evenness also supplies the witness \(\theta=-\log 2\).

For completeness, prove the reflection consumer rather than infer it from any Hilbert--Schmidt estimate. Fix a root \(\mathbf z\in D\), and let \(R_{\mathbf z}=D\cap(2\mathbf z-D)\), with reflection \(\mathbf x\mapsto2\mathbf z-\mathbf x\). Its sole fixed point is \(\mathbf z\); every other site belongs to a two-element reflected pair. Let \(H=\{\mathbf x:\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf x\ge c\}\) be any closed halfspace containing \(\mathbf z\), where \(\mathbf b\ne\mathbf0\). Both sites of a reflected pair cannot be outside \(H\): otherwise adding their two strict inequalities would give \(2\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf z<2c\), contrary to \(\mathbf z\in H\). Boundary sites remain included because the halfspace is closed. Thus, with \(E=R_{\mathbf z}\cap H\), \(|E|\ge(|R_{\mathbf z}|+1)/2\ge|R_{\mathbf z}|/2\).

The log-affine law gives \(p_{\mathbf x}p_{2\mathbf z-\mathbf x}=p_{\mathbf z}^2\) whenever \(\mathbf x\in R_{\mathbf z}\). This identity also follows directly by multiplying the coordinate geometric probabilities. Cauchy--Schwarz and the injectivity of reflection yield

\[
\begin{aligned}
|E|^2
&=\left(\sum_{\mathbf x\in E}\sqrt{p_{\mathbf x}}\,\frac1{\sqrt{p_{\mathbf x}}}\right)^2\\
&\le p(E)\sum_{\mathbf x\in E}\frac1{p_{\mathbf x}}
=\frac{p(E)}{p_{\mathbf z}^2}\sum_{\mathbf x\in E}p_{2\mathbf z-\mathbf x}
\le\frac{p(E)p(R_{\mathbf z})}{p_{\mathbf z}^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(p(D\cap H)\ge p(E)\), every admissible \(H\) satisfies \(p(D\cap H)\ge (|R_{\mathbf z}|+1)^2p_{\mathbf z}^2/(4p(R_{\mathbf z}))\), and hence also the same inequality with \(|R_{\mathbf z}|^2\) in the numerator. Taking the minimum defining \(t_{\mathbf z}=\tau_p(\mathbf z)\), in the normalization of c16327a288b708bd, proves both bounds for the actual depth. No minimizing-cap genericity, full-dimensionality, stationarity, or proxy estimate is needed.

For a Cartesian interval support, put \(j_i=z_i-a_i\) and use the coordinate versions \(r^{(i)}_{j_i},k^{(i)}_{j_i},B^{(i)}_{j_i}\) of the scalar definitions. The exact reflected set is

\[
R_{\mathbf z}
=\prod_{i=1}^N\{z_i-r^{(i)}_{j_i},\ldots,z_i+r^{(i)}_{j_i}\},\qquad
|R_{\mathbf z}|=\prod_i k^{(i)}_{j_i},\qquad
p(R_{\mathbf z})=\prod_i B^{(i)}_{j_i}.
\]

Multiply the rootwise depth bound by \(p_{\mathbf z}\), sum over all roots, and factor the finite product sum:

\[
\begin{aligned}
M_1(p)
&\ge\frac14\sum_{\mathbf z\in D}
\frac{|R_{\mathbf z}|^2p_{\mathbf z}^3}{p(R_{\mathbf z})}\\
&=\frac14\prod_{i=1}^N
\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m_i-1}\frac{(k^{(i)}_j)^2(p^{(i)}_j)^3}{B^{(i)}_j}\right)
=\frac14\prod_i F(m_i,\theta_i).
\end{aligned}
\]

For nonnegative numbers \(x,a\), the identity \(x^3-a^3-3a^2(x-a)=(x-a)^2(x+2a)\ge0\) proves the needed Jensen inequality directly. Apply it with \(x=t_{\mathbf z}\), \(a=M_1(p)\), multiply by \(p_{\mathbf z}\), and sum. Since \(\sum_{\mathbf z}p_{\mathbf z}=1\) and \(\sum_{\mathbf z}p_{\mathbf z}(t_{\mathbf z}-M_1(p))=0\), it gives \(M_3(p)\ge M_1(p)^3\). Cubing the preceding nonnegative bound proves the stated cubic consumer.

On \(D_N=\{0,\ldots,5\}^N\) with the specified product law, every scalar factor is exactly \(423505/861273\). Since \(0<847010/861273<1\), the ratios of the consumer's lower-bound expressions to \(2^{-N}/4\) and \(8^{-N}/64\) are respectively \((847010/861273)^N\) and \((847010/861273)^{3N}\), both tending to zero. This is the claimed exponential obstruction. Even retaining the stronger count \((|R_{\mathbf z}|+1)/2\) in this same Cauchy calculation cannot alone restore a positive absolute prefactor: because \(|R_{\mathbf z}|\ge1\), its summed right-hand side satisfies

\[
\frac14\sum_{\mathbf z\in D_N}
\frac{(|R_{\mathbf z}|+1)^2p_{\mathbf z}^3}{p(R_{\mathbf z})}
\le\sum_{\mathbf z\in D_N}
\frac{|R_{\mathbf z}|^2p_{\mathbf z}^3}{p(R_{\mathbf z})}
=\left(\frac{423505}{861273}\right)^N.
\]

The ratio of this upper bound on that lower-bound expression to \(2^{-N}\) still tends to zero. This does not upper-bound the actual depths or moments. It only identifies the limitation of the proposed scalar-factor reflection/Cauchy route, including its elementary central-site count improvement.
statement:
For every integer \(m\ge1\) and every real \(\theta\), define

\[
Z=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}e^{\theta j},\qquad
p_j=\frac{e^{\theta j}}{Z},\qquad
r_j=\min(j,m-1-j),\qquad
k_j=2r_j+1,\qquad
B_j=\sum_{u=-r_j}^{r_j}p_{j+u}.
\]

The scalar notation is the following specialization of the canonical probability-law notation in accepted fact c16327a288b708bd: \(N=1\), \(D=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\), the scalar \(p_j\) is its \(p_{\mathbf z}\) at \(\mathbf z=j\), and its log-affine parameter is \(\boldsymbol\ell=(\theta)\). Write \(\rho=e^\theta\) for the geometric ratio; this is the test variable called \(q=e^\theta\) in the assignment, not the moment exponent \(q\) in \(M_q\). Define

\[
F(m,\theta)
=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\frac{k_j^2p_j^3}{B_j}
=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}
\frac{p_j^2k_j^2}{\sum_{u=-r_j}^{r_j}e^{\theta u}}.
\]

All denominators are positive, these two formulas agree for every stated parameter, and

\[
F(m,-\theta)=F(m,\theta),\qquad
F(1,\theta)=1,\qquad
F(m,0)=
\begin{cases}
1/2,&m\text{ even},\\
(m^2+1)/(2m^2),&m\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

Nevertheless, \(F(6,\log 2)=423505/861273<1/2\). In particular, any universal lower coefficient for \(F\) is at most \(423505/861273\).

The precise consumer is as follows. Let \(N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb Z\), \(m_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), and \(\theta_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(1\le i\le N\), and set \(D=\prod_{i=1}^N\{a_i,\ldots,a_i+m_i-1\}\). For each coordinate let \(p^{(i)}_j=e^{\theta_i j}/Z_i\) for \(0\le j<m_i\), where \(Z_i=\sum_{j=0}^{m_i-1}e^{\theta_i j}\), and put \(p_{\mathbf z}=\prod_i p^{(i)}_{z_i-a_i}\). Thus the canonical log-affine parameter is \(\boldsymbol\ell=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_N)\); coordinate translation only contributes a constant that cancels in normalization. For \(A\subseteq D\), write \(p(A)=\sum_{\mathbf x\in A}p_{\mathbf x}\). Use exactly the definitions from c16327a288b708bd: \(t_{\mathbf z}=\tau_p(\mathbf z)\) is the minimum of \(p(D\cap H)\) over closed halfspaces \(H\subseteq\mathbb R^N\) containing \(\mathbf z\), and \(M_q(p)=\sum_{\mathbf z\in D}p_{\mathbf z}t_{\mathbf z}^q\) for \(q>0\). Then

\[
M_1(p)\ge\frac14\prod_{i=1}^N F(m_i,\theta_i),\qquad
M_3(p)\ge\frac1{64}\left(\prod_{i=1}^N F(m_i,\theta_i)\right)^3.
\]

Consequently, the false hypothesis \(F(m,\theta)\ge1/2\) for all \(m,\theta\) would have implied \(M_1(p)\ge2^{-N}/4\) and \(M_3(p)\ge8^{-N}/64\) on these Cartesian supports. For the actual supports \(D_N=\{0,\ldots,5\}^N\) and laws \(p_{\mathbf z}=2^{z_1+\cdots+z_N}/63^N\), the two displayed right-hand sides instead equal

\[
\frac{2^{-N}}4\left(\frac{847010}{861273}\right)^N,
\qquad
\frac{8^{-N}}{64}\left(\frac{847010}{861273}\right)^{3N}.
\]

These expressions cannot certify the corresponding dimensional rates with any fixed positive absolute prefactor. No claim is made that the actual \(M_1(p)\) or \(M_3(p)\) violates those rates, or that a different reflection estimate cannot establish them.
